reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard haematology references
clinicalPearls: An inherited bone marrow failure syndrome that combines exocrine pancreatic insufficiency with cytopenias, most consistently neutropenia
Most cases are autosomal recessive and caused by biallelic mutations in the SBDS gene, another disorder of ribosome maturation
Children typically present with fatty stools and failure to thrive from pancreatic insufficiency, plus recurrent infections from neutropenia
Skeletal abnormalities such as metaphyseal dysostosis and short stature are characteristic associated features
Neutropenia may be intermittent, and pancytopenia can develop; the marrow is often hypocellular
Pancreatic function tends to improve with age even though the enzyme deficiency and skeletal features persist
There is a significant risk of progression to myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukaemia

Management principles include pancreatic enzyme replacement and fat-soluble vitamin support, infection prophylaxis and treatment, haematological support, and allogeneic stem cell transplantation for severe marrow failure or malignant transformation
It must be distinguished from cystic fibrosis, which also causes pancreatic insufficiency but has a normal sweat chloride in SDS
reference.pathophysiology: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome is most often caused by biallelic mutations in SBDS, a gene whose product is required for the maturation of the large ribosomal subunit and ribosome function. The resulting defect in ribosome biogenesis impairs highly proliferative and secretory tissues, producing exocrine pancreatic acinar failure with fatty replacement, ineffective haematopoiesis with neutropenia and marrow hypocellularity, and skeletal developmental abnormalities. Genomic and clonal instability in the haematopoietic compartment underlies the predisposition to myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Cystic fibrosis (pancreatic insufficiency with abnormal sweat chloride)
Other inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (Fanconi anaemia, dyskeratosis congenita)
Acquired causes of neutropenia or pancreatic insufficiency
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and serial monitoring for neutropenia and other cytopenias
Tests of exocrine pancreatic function (e.g. faecal elastase, serum trypsinogen and isoamylase)
Sweat chloride testing to exclude cystic fibrosis
Bone marrow examination with cytogenetics to assess cellularity and clonal change
Molecular genetic testing of SBDS and related genes; skeletal imaging
redFlags: Severe neutropenia with serious or recurrent infection
Progression to pancytopenia or marrow failure
New cytogenetic clonal abnormalities or blasts indicating MDS or acute leukaemia
Failure to thrive with malnutrition and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
reference.prognosis: Pancreatic insufficiency is manageable and often improves with age, but the long-term prognosis is dominated by the risk of progressive marrow failure and transformation to myelodysplasia or acute myeloid leukaemia. Stem cell transplantation can address the haematological disease, and overall survival depends heavily on whether clonal evolution occurs.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the pancreatic insufficiency as cystic fibrosis
Overlooking intermittent neutropenia because counts fluctuate
Failing to monitor the marrow for clonal evolution over time
Neglecting nutritional and fat-soluble vitamin support
Not screening potential related stem cell donors for the disorder
management: Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy with fat-soluble vitamin supplementation for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and steatorrhoea
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor for severe or symptomatic neutropenia, with prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics for febrile illness given the infection risk
Serial full blood counts and periodic bone marrow examination with cytogenetics to detect evolving marrow failure, myelodysplasia or acute myeloid leukaemia
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for progressive marrow failure or leukaemic transformation
Nutritional support with monitoring of growth and correction of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
Coordinated care across haematology, gastroenterology, orthopaedics and dietetics for the skeletal and multisystem features
Genetic counselling and cascade family testing given autosomal recessive SBDS inheritance
